hints: Recall that velocity is the integral of acceleration with respect to time: $v = \int a\,dt$.
Integrate $a = kt^{1/2}$ to obtain $v = \frac{2}{3}kt^{3/2} + c$, using $v(0) = 0$ to show $c = 0$.
Substitute $t = 9$ and $v = 1.8$ into $v(t) = \frac{2}{3}kt^{3/2}$ to show that $18k = 1.8$ and hence $k = 0.1$.
walkthrough:
Integrate the acceleration function to find velocity:
$$v = \int kt^{1/2}\,dt = \frac{2}{3}kt^{3/2} + c$$
$$\text{Since the particle starts from rest at } t = 0,\quad c = 0 \implies v = \frac{2}{3}kt^{3/2}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
State the calculus relationship between velocity and acceleration: velocity is the indefinite integral of acceleration with respect to time:
$$v = \int a\,dt$$

Substitute $a = kt^{1/2}$ and integrate using the power rule $\int t^n\,dt = \frac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}$:
$$v = k\left(\frac{t^{3/2}}{3/2}\right) + c = \frac{2}{3}kt^{3/2} + c$$

Apply the initial condition that the particle starts from rest at $t = 0$ ($v(0) = 0$):
$$0 = \frac{2}{3}k(0)^{3/2} + c \implies c = 0$$
$$v(t) = \frac{2}{3}kt^{3/2}$$

Divide both sides by 18 to confirm $k$:
$$k = \frac{1.8}{18} = 0.1$$

hints: Integrate the first velocity function $v = \frac{1}{15}t^{3/2}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 9$ to find the distance in the first 9 s.
Evaluate the first integral to get $s_1 = \frac{2}{75}(9^{5/2}) = 6.48\text{ m}$.
Integrate the second velocity function $v = 0.2(t-9)^2 + 1.8$ from $t = 9$ to $t = 18$ to find $s_2$.
walkthrough:
Integrate velocity from $t = 0$ to $t = 9$ to find distance $s_1$:
$$s_1 = \int_0^9 \frac{2}{3}(0.1)t^{3/2}\,dt = \left[\frac{2}{3}(0.1)\left(\frac{t^{5/2}}{2.5}\right)\right]_0^9 = \left[\frac{2}{75}t^{5/2}\right]_0^9$$
$$s_1 = \frac{2}{75}(9)^{5/2} = \frac{2}{75}(243) = 6.48\text{ m}$$

Compare the two distances:
$$\frac{s_1}{s_2} = \frac{6.48}{64.8} = \frac{1}{10}$$
$$\text{Hence the distance travelled in the first 9 seconds is one tenth of the distance from } t=9 \text{ to } t=18.$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Name the relationship: distance is found by integrating the velocity function between the given time boundaries:
$$s = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,dt$$

For the first stage ($0 \leq t \leq 9$), substitute $k = 0.1$ into the velocity function: $v_1(t) = \frac{2}{3}(0.1)t^{3/2} = \frac{1}{15}t^{3/2}$:
$$s_1 = \int_0^9 \frac{1}{15}t^{3/2}\,dt = \left[\frac{1}{15} \times \frac{t^{5/2}}{5/2}\right]_0^9 = \left[\frac{2}{75}t^{5/2}\right]_0^9$$
$$9^{5/2} = (\sqrt{9})^5 = 3^5 = 243$$
$$s_1 = \frac{2}{75} \times 243 = \frac{486}{75} = 6.48\text{ m}$$

Compare the two calculated values:
$$s_1 = 6.48\text{ m},\quad s_2 = 64.8\text{ m}$$
$$6.48 = \frac{1}{10} \times 64.8$$
$$\text{Thus, } s_1 \text{ is exactly one tenth of } s_2.$$

hints: In the first phase ($0 \le t \le 9$), $a_1(t) = 0.1t^{1/2}$; evaluate its maximum at $t = 9$.
In the second phase ($9 \le t \le 10$), differentiate $v_2 = 0.2(t-9)^2 + 1.8$ to find $a_2(t) = 0.4(t-9)$, and evaluate at $t = 10$.
Compare the peak acceleration of both phases: $0.3\text{ m s}^{-2}$ vs $0.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to determine the greatest acceleration.
walkthrough:
Find the maximum acceleration in the first phase ($0 \leq t \leq 9$) where $a_1 = 0.1t^{1/2}$:
$$a_{1,\text{max}} = a_1(9) = 0.1(9)^{1/2} = 0.1(3) = 0.3\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Differentiate velocity in the second phase to find acceleration for $9 \leq t \leq 10$:
$$a_2 = \frac{d}{dt}[0.2(t-9)^2 + 1.8] = 0.4(t-9)$$

Evaluate at $t = 10\text{ s}$ and compare:
$$a_2(10) = 0.4(10 - 9) = 0.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
$$\text{Since } 0.4 > 0.3,\text{ the greatest acceleration is } 0.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Examine the acceleration in Phase 1 ($0 \leq t \leq 9$), given by $a_1(t) = 0.1t^{1/2}$. Because the square root function is strictly increasing, its greatest value occurs at $t = 9\text{ s}$:
$$a_{1,\text{max}} = 0.1\sqrt{9} = 0.1(3) = 0.3\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Find the acceleration function in Phase 2 ($9 \leq t \leq 10$) by differentiating its velocity $v_2(t) = 0.2(t-9)^2 + 1.8$ with respect to $t$:
$$a_2(t) = \frac{dv_2}{dt} = 0.2 \times 2(t-9) = 0.4(t-9)$$

Because $a_2(t)$ is an increasing linear function for $t \geq 9$, its maximum over the interval $[9, 10]$ occurs at $t = 10\text{ s}$:
$$a_2(10) = 0.4(10 - 9) = 0.4(1) = 0.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Compare the maximum accelerations from both phases:
$$0.4\text{ m s}^{-2} > 0.3\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
$$\text{Therefore, the greatest acceleration during the first 10 seconds is } 0.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
